title: Quantization Profile Library (QPL) — Overview
author: Arjun Desai
body:
## Purpose
The Quantization Profile Library (QPL) is Redwood Inference’s opt-in catalog of **Redwood-published, versioned quantization profiles** that can be selectively enabled at the **API route level**.

The intent is to make quantization:
- **Cheaper**: reduce $/1M tokens (or increase tokens/$) for supported models.
- **Safer**: allow route-scoped canaries and fast rollback when quality regressions are workload-specific.
- **Standardized**: one schema, one validation process, and one distribution mechanism across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private.

This page is a high-level overview. Implementation and requirements are covered in linked pages.

---

## What is a “quantization profile”?
A quantization profile is a signed, versioned artifact in the model registry that describes a specific **servable model variant** and the constraints required to run it reliably.

A profile is not just “int8” or “int4”; it is a complete recipe that includes:
- **Quantization type + method** (e.g., bf16 baseline, fp16, int8 weight-only, int4 weight-only; method details may vary by model family)
- **Runtime execution constraints**
  - Compatible kernels / backends
  - GPU architecture constraints (e.g., H100 vs A10)
  - Max sequence length / KV cache constraints where applicable
  - Known incompatibilities and fallback behavior
- **Calibration & provenance**
  - Calibration dataset notes (what was used and what was not)
  - Build tooling version(s) used to generate the artifact
  - Links to eval and perf reports
- **Expected deltas**
  - Latency and throughput expectations by sequence-length regime
  - Cost delta expectations (used for customer guidance and internal success metrics)

A profile is always scoped to:
- A specific **base model** (and optionally a pinned base model build)
- A specific **quantization variant**
- A specific set of **hardware + kernel constraints**

---

## Why QPL is opt-in and route-scoped
Quantization can produce workload-specific regressions (e.g., tool calling / JSON mode formatting drift, long-context degradation, rare-token errors). As a result:

- QPL is **opt-in**: no customer is opted in by default in v1.
- Controls are **route-scoped** (not only model-scoped): customers can enable quantization only for workloads that tolerate it (e.g., batch summarization) while keeping interactive chat routes on baseline.
- Rollout supports **canary-by-percentage** and rapid rollback via the control plane.

For rationale and rollout model details, see: ADR: “Quantization Profiles — opt-in and route-scoped”.

---

## Supported model families (initial library)
QPL support expands over time. “Supported” means we have a published profile that meets Redwood acceptance thresholds and has been validated on at least one approved GPU class.

### Initial target families (MVP / Beta)
- **Llama-family** instruction-tuned chat models (common production workloads; well-understood kernels)
- **Mistral-family** instruction-tuned chat models

### Expansion targets (post-beta)
- Long-context optimized variants within supported families (requires dedicated long-context prompt-set coverage)
- Additional open model families as kernel maturity and eval coverage improve

### What is explicitly not supported in v1
- Customer-supplied arbitrary profiles (QPL is Redwood-published only in v1)
- “Auto-quantize everything” default-on behavior
- Profiles without hardware scoping and perf/eval attachments

Notes:
- Each profile is **hardware-scoped**. A “model family is supported” does not imply “supported on all GPUs.”
- Compatibility is enforced by runtime checks; incompatibility triggers fallback to baseline (with metrics).

---

## Versioning strategy (how profiles change safely)
Profiles use **semantic versioning** (SemVer) with additional immutable identifiers for auditability.

### Identifiers
- **profile_id**: stable identifier for a (model, variant, hardware-scope) tuple
- **version**: SemVer, used for compatibility and controlled upgrades
- **artifact_digest**: immutable content hash for integrity verification

### SemVer guidelines (high level)
- **PATCH**: bugfixes that do not change numerical behavior materially (e.g., metadata corrections, compatibility annotation fixes, tooling changes that preserve outputs within acceptance thresholds)
- **MINOR**: improvements that may change performance/latency but remain within quality thresholds (e.g., kernel change, better packing, improved calibration that does not exceed regression limits)
- **MAJOR**: changes that may alter behavior enough to require explicit re-validation or customer re-approval (e.g., changed quantization method, materially different numerics, or expanded constraints)

### Publication stages
Profiles may be tagged internally as:
- **experimental**: internal use only; may not meet full acceptance thresholds
- **beta**: available for opt-in customers under beta terms; requires full eval/perf attachments and rollback readiness
- **ga**: meets published acceptance thresholds; eligible for broader opt-in

The schema and compatibility expectations are defined in “Profile Schema and Versioning”.

---

## Ownership and operating model
QPL is cross-functional; publishing is gated.

### Primary owners
- **Applied ML / Performance & Evals** (profile methodology, calibration notes, quality gates): Arjun Desai (DRI), Karthik Iyer, Jonas Weber
- **Serving Runtime** (execution path, kernel compatibility, fallback safety): Mateo Alvarez, Hiro Tanaka
- **Smart Routing / Platform** (route policy evaluation, precedence model): Mina Haddad, Ravi Menon

### Approvals (minimum)
A profile can be published to the customer-visible library only when:
- Quality gates are met and approved by Applied ML / Evals
- Runtime compatibility is verified on the scoped GPU matrix
- Security requirements for signing and permissions are satisfied

### SRE readiness
SRE owns rollout/rollback operational readiness requirements:
- Canary support and safe disable primitives
- Alerting and dashboards segmented by route + profile
- Incident response procedures (see rollback runbook)

---

## How profiles are consumed (control plane → routing → runtime)
QPL integrates into the request path without requiring per-request user input.

### High-level flow
1) **Admin config (Console/API)**: Customer enables quantization on a specific route (optionally with canary percentage and allowlist conditions).
2) **Policy evaluation (routing layer)**: For a given request, routing evaluates:
   - Is quantization enabled for this route (and for this org/customer)?
   - Is the request in-canary (percentage gate)?
   - Is there an override (force baseline) due to incident, regression, or compatibility signal?
3) **Runtime resolution**: If eligible, runtime resolves the best matching profile based on:
   - Requested model
   - Hardware class / GPU arch
   - Sequence-length regime (when applicable)
   - Kernel/backend availability
4) **Compatibility checks**:
   - If compatible: execute quantized kernel path
   - If incompatible: fall back to baseline safely (no customer-visible failure solely due to quantization)
5) **Telemetry**: Emit metrics/tags for:
   - quantization_enabled (policy)
   - quantization_applied (runtime)
   - profile_id + version
   - fallback_reason (if baseline fallback happens)

### Key design principle: “Policy decides intent; runtime decides feasibility.”
- The control plane and routing policy determine whether a request is *allowed* to use quantization.
- The runtime determines whether it is *safe and compatible* to apply a specific profile at execution time.

---

## Safety guardrails (what prevents bad rollouts)
QPL includes multiple layers of guardrails:

- **Pre-publish gates**
  - Baseline vs quantized eval comparisons on approved prompt sets
  - Perf benchmarks across GPU SKUs and sequence-length bins
  - Signed artifacts and restricted publish permissions

- **During rollout**
  - Route-level opt-in + canary percentage
  - Audit logs for every config change
  - Dashboards segmented by route/profile

- **Auto-disable and fast rollback**
  - Signals from eval harness and production monitoring can automatically disable quantization for impacted routes
  - Clear runbook for manual rollback (including cache invalidation when needed)

See:
- “Profile Validation & Quality Gates”
- “Quantization Profile Acceptance Thresholds”
- “Quantization Profile Rollback Runbook”

---

## What customers see (product surface)
In v1, customers interact with QPL via:
- **Console**: per-route toggle + canary percentage + warnings + linkouts to metrics
- **Config API**: read/write route quantization settings (RBAC + audit logging)
- **Observability**: tags indicating whether a route/request is running baseline or quantized, and which profile was used

Customers do not upload profiles in v1 and do not need to pass request headers to opt in (route config is the primary control).

---

## Definitions
- **Baseline**: Redwood’s default non-quantized execution path for a model on a given hardware class.
- **Quantized execution**: Runtime path that uses a QPL profile and compatible kernels.
- **Route**: A customer-defined API route/config object used to separate workloads (e.g., “interactive-chat”, “batch-summarize”, “rerank”).
- **Fallback**: Execution on baseline kernels because quantization is disabled by policy or not feasible by runtime compatibility checks.

---

## FAQ
### Does enabling quantization on a route guarantee it will be used?
No. Enabling quantization expresses intent; runtime will apply quantization only when it can resolve a compatible profile for the request and hardware. Otherwise it falls back to baseline.

### Can a profile be used across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private?
Yes, provided the hardware/kernels match the profile’s constraints and the profile is available in the respective registry environment. Private deployments may have a smaller allowed set depending on compliance posture and pinned versions.

### How do we avoid “silent” quality degradation?
- Pre-publish eval gating on prompt sets and acceptance thresholds
- Route-level canary rollout
- Telemetry that differentiates “enabled” vs “applied” and records profile_id/version
- Auto-disable hooks on regression signals
